The isAccessTokenId method returns false when the grant shortcut matches the expected shortcut, inverting the match logic. This causes all four callers (expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) to pass for any token whose grant shortcut differs from the expected one, so the assertions no longer validate the grant portion of the token ID.

issues.descricao: The AccessTokenContext constructor checks grantType twice instead of rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId passes validation and is encoded as ':null'.
issues.textoGolden: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the constructor validates `grantType` a second time instead of `rawTokenId` (`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`). WHY: a null `rawTokenId` is silently accepted, so `encodeTokenId` produces a token id ending in `:null` and any later consumer of the raw id gets an invalid value instead of an early failure. HOW: change the argument to `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

Line 73 calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") — it validates grantType a second time (line 72 already does) with a message naming a different field. rawTokenId is never validated, so a null rawTokenId is accepted at construction and the advertised check/message is wrong. It should be Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed").

The null-check message names the wrong parameter: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` validates `grantType` but reports `rawTokenId`, and it duplicates the check on line 72 while `rawTokenId` is never validated at all. The message that reaches the reader contradicts the code it guards; it should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

issues.descricao: isAccessTokenId reads the grant shortcut at the wrong offset (3,5 instead of 4,6) and inverts the comparison, so the event assertions never verify the token's grant type.
issues.textoGolden: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `isAccessTokenId` reads the grant shortcut from the wrong offset and inverts the comparison — `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. WHY: for the encoded id `ssttgg:raw` the grant shortcut occupies 0-based indices 4-5, so `substring(3,5)` inspects the token-type/grant boundary and can never equal the expected shortcut; combined with the inverted `return false`, the equality branch is unreachable and the matcher validates only the UUID part. As a result the new assertions in `expectCodeToToken`/`expectRefresh`/`expectDeviceCodeToToken`/`expectAuthReqIdToToken` do not actually assert the grant type and would pass even if the grant shortcut were wrong. HOW: use `items[0].substring(4, 6)` and negate the condition (`if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`).

The matcher logic is inverted: line 483 returns false when the extracted grant shortcut EQUALS expectedGrantShortcut, so a token that actually carries the expected grant fails the matcher, while a token with any other grant shortcut falls through and passes. The condition should be negated: `if (!items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. Also note the encode site writes the grant shortcut at chars 4-6 (substring(4,6)); substring(3,5) reads one character early into the token-type field, so the offset is off by one relative to TokenManager.encodeTokenId.

The comment 'Grant type shortcut starts at character 4th char' disagrees with the encoding that this PR defines (sessionType chars 1-2, tokenType 3-4, grantType 5-6, e.g. 'trltcc'), and the code reads substring(3,5) — the 4th-5th chars, i.e. the token-type second char plus the grant first char, never the grant shortcut. The comment (and the index) should point at the 5th char / substring(4,6).

issues.descricao: getShortcut() Javadoc says shortcuts are usually 3 letters, but the encoding requires exactly 2-character shortcuts.
issues.textoGolden: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.

comentarios.texto: The Javadoc says getShortcut() returns 'usually like 3-letters shortcut', but every implementation introduced in this PR returns a 2-character shortcut ('ac','cc','pg','pc','rt','ro','te','ci','dg') and the encoder relies on exactly 2 chars (encoded context length 6 = 2+2+2). The doc states a length the code does not produce; it should say 2-character shortcut.

Grant shortcuts are registered without enforcing the two-character length required by the decoder. A custom grant returning a three-character shortcut, which the new OAuth2GrantTypeFactory documentation explicitly suggests, produces a seven-character prefix that getTokenContextFromTokenId rejects, breaking encode/decode round trips for that grant. Validate shortcut length during registration and dynamic refresh, and document the required two-character format.

The new contract describes getShortcut() as usually returning a three-letter shortcut, but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider requires exactly two characters for the grant field (six total prefix characters, decoded with substring(4, 6)). An extension author following this documentation can produce token IDs that the default decoder rejects. Document the required two-character length rather than advertising three letters.

issues.descricao: testIncorrectGrantType catches any RuntimeException, so it passes on a NullPointerException from the unset sessionFactory rather than verifying the unknown-grant IllegalArgumentException.
issues.textoGolden: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

comentarios.texto: Catching RuntimeException allows this negative test to pass for an unrelated fixture failure. The fixture constructs the factory without postInit, leaving sessionFactory null; resolving the unregistered `ac` shortcut calls sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream and throws NullPointerException before the decoder's intended unknown-grant IllegalArgumentException. Catch/assert IllegalArgumentException specifically and provide a factory fixture whose lookup returns no matching grant, so removing the decoder's validation would fail the test.

issues.descricao: Client-credentials (and UMA permission) token issuance never sets the GRANT_TYPE attribute, so their access token ids are encoded with the unknown grant 'na' instead of their shortcut.

comentarios.texto: The new grant metadata falls back to 'na' for client-credentials and UMA tokens because their issuance paths never set Constants.GRANT_TYPE on their fresh ClientSessionContext. ClientCredentialsGrantType calls responseBuilder.generateAccessToken directly, and PermissionGrantType delegates to AuthorizationTokenService, so neither executes the new assignment in createTokenResponse; tokens from these known grants therefore carry unknown grant context. Set the grant attribute in both issuance paths before generating the access token.

issues.descricao: Lazy registration of newly deployed grants does not check shortcut uniqueness, so a grant reusing an existing shortcut silently overwrites the reverse mapping and older tokens decode to the wrong grant.

comentarios.texto: Enforce shortcut uniqueness during lazy registration rather than overwriting grantsByShortcuts. If a newly deployed grant B uses existing grant A's shortcut, this path replaces shortcut→A with shortcut→B while retaining both forward entries. Previously issued A tokens then decode as B. Concurrent registrations of two new grants with the same shortcut likewise both succeed, with the last inverse-map write winning. Use collision-aware atomic registration and reject the conflicting grant before publishing its forward mapping.

issues.descricao: getShortcut() is added as an abstract method to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory without a default, breaking existing custom grant type factories (compile error or AbstractMethodError when DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit calls it).

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: getCredentials() rebuilds the recovery-codes model with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...), which hashes the codes and always reproduces them in original order, so the model returned by the federated store never reflects consumed codes. WHY: RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean derives the 'next code to enter' number from this model and RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator relies on allCodesUsed() to decide whether to remove the credential; with a freshly rebuilt model the displayed code number can be stale and the removal branch is driven by clone state rather than persisted state, producing wrong results for federated users. HOW: Persist and rehydrate the hashed secretData (and consumed-code state) instead of regenerating it from the raw list on each read.

issues.descricao: The test user-storage provider validates recovery codes without consuming the used code, so the same code can be replayed.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new recovery-codes branch of isValid only checks whether the submitted code appears in the stored list and never removes the consumed entry. WHY: Unlike the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid (which calls removeRecoveryAuthnCode()+updateStoredCredential), the federated path never consumes a code and allCodesUsed() can never become true, so a used recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely. HOW: On a successful match, remove that entry from the stored codes (rewrite recoveryCodes.credentialData), mirroring the local provider's consume-on-success semantics.

The new recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list without consuming the accepted code. Repeating a successful login with the same code succeeds indefinitely, while getCredentials reconstructs all original codes so the login form never advances or detects exhaustion. Validate the next unused code and persist its consumption before returning success.

The new federated recovery-code validator accepts any code in the original list but never removes a successfully used code from myUser.recoveryCodes. Consequently the same recovery code remains valid on subsequent logins, and getCredentials reconstructs the full original set every time. Consume and persist the successfully validated code (and test a second login/replay), so federated recovery codes retain their one-time semantics.

issues.descricao: getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-codes credential without copying the stored credential id, so the returned federated credential has a null id and cannot be targeted by id-based removal.
issues.textoGolden: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: getCredentials builds the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel via createFromValues but never sets its id from the stored myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() (createFromValues does not populate id). WHY: The returned federated model has a null id, so callers that identify/delete the credential by id — e.g. RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) when all codes are used, or federated-credential deletion via getFederatedCredentialsStream — cannot target the actual credential. HOW: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after createFromValues.

getCredentials rebuilds the recovery-code model without copying the ID assigned during updateCredential. createFromValues does not assign an ID, so the exposed federated credential has a null ID and CredentialDeleteHelper cannot resolve it by the stored credential ID for account deletion. Copy myUser.recoveryCodes.getId() to the reconstructed model before returning it.

The CredentialModel returned from getCredentials for recovery codes is built with createFromValues and never gets the stored credential's id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()). RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator later calls removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId()) once all codes are used, and this would pass a null id. Fix: call model.setId(myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()) after creating the model.

issues.descricao: Creating recovery codes in external storage does not remove a previously stored local recovery-codes credential, and validation falls back to local storage, so the replaced codes still authenticate.

comentarios.texto: Successful recovery-code creation in external storage leaves any existing locally stored recovery-code credential active. For a federated user who previously stored codes locally and now has an external provider supporting this type, regeneration no longer calls RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential's replacement cleanup; UserCredentialManager.isValid falls back to the local validator when external validation rejects an old code, so the supposedly replaced codes still authenticate. Remove the previous local recovery-code credential after successful external creation.

issues.descricao: Exhausted recovery codes are removed with removeStoredCredentialById, which only covers local storage, so a federated recovery-codes credential is never removed.

comentarios.texto: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() can now return a credential from user storage (federated), but this code still calls removeStoredCredentialById() on it once all codes are used. That removal only targets local stored credentials, so a federated credential may not be removed. The user could then be left with an exhausted credential in user storage. Remove federated credentials through the federated path, or confirm the removal reaches user storage.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a credential from user storage, but exhausted codes are cleaned up with removeStoredCredentialById, which only targets the local DB. For a federated credential (possibly with a null id), the exhausted credential is never removed or the call misbehaves, so the user keeps a dead credential. Remove federated credentials through a path that covers user storage, for example by checking where the credential came from.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can now return a federated credential. The authenticator still removes an exhausted one with removeStoredCredentialById(getId()), which only deletes from the local store, and the federated model's id may be null. Remove the credential through the path that matches where it was found, for example by checking whether it came from the federated stream and using the federated removal.

issues.descricao: Looking up recovery codes now always queries the federated provider first, which for LDAP users adds an LDAP round-trip and can throw IllegalStateException, failing recovery-code login with a 500.
An error log in the test user storage hard-codes the credential type as 'recovery-codes' instead of using RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE ('recovery-authn-codes').

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `canDelete` now ORs in the prom-based delete ability, but the Delete menu item is still gated on `rulerRule` being present (line 165), which is always undefined in the list view that this PR switches to promRule. WHY: For Grafana rules rendered from the list view (`GrafanaRuleListItem` → `RuleActionsButtons.V2` passes only `promRule`), the newly computed `grafanaDeleteAbility` is dead and Delete silently never appears, even when the user has delete permission. HOW: Render the Delete item when `canDelete` is true and gate on the presence of a resolvable identifier (already guaranteed non-null here), not on `rulerRule`; when only `promRule` is available, call the delete handler with the prom-derived identifier.

issues.descricao: The pause menu item is still gated on a Grafana ruler rule, but the list view now passes only the Prometheus rule, so Pause/Resume disappears for list-view rules even when the user may pause them.

comentarios.texto: The new Prometheus-based pause ability cannot display Pause or Resume for list-view rules because the menu still requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) before rendering MenuItemPauseRule. GrafanaRuleListItem now supplies only promRule, so these actions disappear even for editable rules. Adapt the pause menu item to accept the Grafana identifier and Prometheus pause state, or load the ruler rule on demand.

issues.descricao: The Delete menu item still requires a ruler rule, which list-view Grafana rules no longer provide, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action.

comentarios.texto: The new Prometheus-based delete ability is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule` when rendering the Delete item. Both Grafana list-view paths now omit rulerRule, so users with delete permission lose the Delete action entirely. Render deletion using the available identifier and group identifier instead of requiring the ruler DTO, adapting the callback contract accordingly.

issues.descricao: When the Grafana prom-rule branch is skipped (datasource rules), useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) still reports Duplicate as supported and allowed by Grafana create permission, and AlertRuleMenu ORs it with the ruler ability, so Duplicate appears on cloud rules even when the ruler check denies it.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: canDuplicate ORs ruler ability with grafana ability where grafana path is skipToken=>undefined for cloud rules, and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) returns Duplicate=[true,true] whenever the user has global Grafana create permission. WHY: Any user with Grafana rule-create gets Duplicate menu item on cloud/Mimir rules even when ruler abilities deny it — incorrect authorization gating. HOW: Return NotSupported for all abilities when rule is skipToken/undefined, or gate grafana branch on prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(promRule) before ORing.

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities returns AlwaysSupported for Duplicate when rule is undefined (skipToken): loading is false from the !rule early-return, so MaybeSupported=true and duplicateSupported=true. ORed in AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons this leaks Grafana create permission into non-Grafana rules. Gate MaybeSupported/duplicateSupported on rule existence (e.g. NotSupported when !rule).

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities must return NotSupported for all actions when rule is undefined (skipToken). Currently MaybeSupported falls back to AlwaysSupported when !loading, so Duplicate=[true, global-create] is true for a cloud rule passed as skipToken, and AlertRuleMenu/RuleActionsButtons OR-logic then incorrectly enables Duplicate (and Explore). Guard with if (!rule) return all-NotSupported abilities or make MaybeSupported require rule.

issues.descricao: The refactor of useAllAlertRuleAbilities into useAllRulerRuleAbilities drops the isFederatedRuleGroup check (isFederated is hardcoded false), so federated Mimir rules are reported as editable and deletable.

comentarios.texto: useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated = false. The previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check is gone, so federated Mimir rules are no longer treated as immutable and can show edit and delete abilities. Keep the federation check in this wrapper, or pass the federation state into the shared hook.

Delegating useAllAlertRuleAbilities to useAllRulerRuleAbilities discards the group's federation status and replaces the previous isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) check with a constant false. Legacy RuleActionsButtons consequently enables editing rules in groups with source_tenants, although these groups were explicitly immutable before this change. Preserve the CombinedRule federation check in the wrapper or pass federation status into the delegated ability calculation.

Preserve the federated-group immutability check when delegating this CombinedRule hook. Previously useAllAlertRuleAbilities inspected rule.group with isFederatedRuleGroup and disabled modification/removal for federated rules. The replacement delegates to a hook that hardcodes isFederated=false and receives no group information. Existing useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities consumers therefore now receive supported update/delete abilities for federated rules when datasource permissions allow them, exposing operations that the previous contract explicitly prohibited. Pass the federation state through or retain that restriction in this wrapper.

issues.descricao: The Grafana prom-rule abilities gate Pause, Restore, Export and DeletePermanently on alertingRule(rule) while the comment claims it checks Grafana-managed rules, so Grafana recording rules lose these actions in the list view.

comentarios.texto: The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the variable it describes is `isAlertingRule`. That variable is true only for alerting rules and false for Grafana recording rules. Fix the comment, or rename the variable, so it says the check is for alerting rules. As written, readers will expect Pause, Export and Silence to be enabled for recording rules.

The comment says all GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed, but the check used is alertingRule(rule), which is false for recording rules. Pause, Restore, ModifyExport and DeletePermanently are therefore wrongly disabled for Grafana recording rules, where the old isGrafanaManagedAlertRule check allowed them. Use prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule) for these abilities, and keep alertingRule only for Silence.

issues.descricao: The comment claims GrafanaPromRuleDTO abilities have no loading state, but the next line makes support depend on the folder loading flag.

comentarios.texto: The comment says there is no loading state, but the next line is `loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported`. `loading` comes from the folder fetch. Update the comment to say that support depends on the folder loading state.

issues.descricao: The Grafana branch of the filtered rule list renders GrafanaRuleListItem without a key prop, so React reconciles the streaming list by index and warns about missing keys.
issues.textoGolden: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The grafana branch of the filtered list renders <GrafanaRuleListItem .../> without a `key` prop, dropping the `key={key}` that the replaced <GrafanaRuleLoader key={key} .../> had. WHY: `rules.map` renders a dynamic list keyed by getRuleKey/hashRule; without a key React logs duplicate-key warnings and reconciles rows by index, so as the async rule stream updates/reorders the wrong rule row can be reused/mutated (stale state, swapped actions). HOW: add `key={key}` (the value is already destructured on line 152) to the <GrafanaRuleListItem> element.

WHAT: Grafana branch of FilterViewResults renders GrafanaRuleListItem without key={key} while datasource and unknown branches pass key. WHY: Breaks React list reconciliation — wrong item reuse, stale actions/state and console key warnings for every Grafana hit. HOW: Add key={key} to the GrafanaRuleListItem element.

issues.descricao: The test named 'should render More button with action menu options' only checks the More button exists, never the menu options.

comentarios.texto: The test 'should render More button with action menu options' only checks that the More button exists. It finds the button by name 'More', so the aria-label and text assertions are tautological. It would pass even if the menu had no actions or the abilities were broken. Click the button and assert the expected menu items, or rename the test to match what it checks.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never verifies any action menu option: the body only asserts the More button exists and has aria-label/text 'More'. It would still pass if the dropdown were rendered empty (Silence/Duplicate/Copy link/Export all missing), i.e. the behaviour the name promises is not covered. Either open the menu and assert the menu items, or rename the test to reflect that it only checks the trigger button's rendering/accessibility.

Test named 'should render More button with action menu options' never opens the menu nor asserts menu items — it only checks More button presence/aria/text. Click More and assert expected menuitems (or rename to 'should render More button') so it fails if menu actions break.

issues.descricao: GrafanaGroupLoader's JSDoc still says it loads from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints after the ruler query was removed.

comentarios.texto: The JSDoc for GrafanaGroupLoader still says "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints." but this PR removed the ruler API query entirely — the component now only calls useGetGrafanaGroupsQuery (Prometheus). The documentation describes a data source the function no longer consumes; update it to state only the Prometheus endpoint is loaded (and the same stale "Ruler response" reference in the expectedRulesCount prop doc at lines 18–19 should be corrected).

issues.descricao: For list-view Grafana rules RuleActionsButtons gets only promRule, so the Silence menu item is shown but the silence drawer, still gated on a ruler alerting rule, never renders and clicking Silence does nothing.
issues.textoGolden: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

comentarios.texto: Passing only promRule enables the Silence notifications menu item but leaves RuleActionsButtons.V2 unable to render its silence drawer, which is guarded by rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule). Clicking Silence only updates showSilenceDrawer and displays nothing because rule is undefined. Update the drawer to accept a rule UID—the inspected SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only needs grafana_alert.uid—and allow the Prometheus alerting-rule path to render it.

The new list item passes only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, but that component renders SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer only under `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. With rule undefined, clicking the newly enabled 'Silence notifications' action only sets state and never opens a drawer. Adapt the silence rendering path to load/use the rule by its Prometheus identifier before switching this caller to promRule-only.

WHAT: getEditableIdentifier now enables a prom-only path (Grafana uid identifier with rulerRule undefined) but the silence drawer still renders only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. WHY: In the list view Silence menu item can be shown via grafana abilities, clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer but the drawer never mounts, so Silence silently does nothing. HOW: Gate the drawer on promRule as well or provide a prom-based silence drawer.

issues.descricao: RulesTable RBAC tests only mock useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities and leave useRulerRuleAbilities denied, so the ruler-based Delete permission branch of AlertRuleMenu is never tested.
A stray '// duplicate' comment was left next to useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable(rule) in useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: the flush-side span-count cap was removed from `_load_segment_data` while `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is now assigned at line 158 but never read. WHY: the configured limit silently does nothing — any change to `max_segment_spans` (or its callers) will not limit segments, and the only cap is the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua, so an operator tuning the Python value gets no effect and oversized segments flush. HOW: either remove `max_segment_spans` entirely, or pass the limit into the Lua eviction (e.g. as an ARGV) so the single source of truth is honored.

issues.descricao: ZUNIONSTORE merges sorted sets with the default SUM aggregate, so a span payload present in both keys gets a doubled end-timestamp score and is wrongly kept by the oldest-first eviction.

comentarios.texto: ZUNIONSTORE uses AGGREGATE SUM by default, so when the same span payload is present in both `set_key` and the merged `span_key`/`parent_key` (duplicate delivery is anticipated by this buffer's own comments), its score is added instead of being kept equal to `end_timestamp_precise`. Because eviction at line 63 (`zpopmin` by score) compares scores across all members of `set_key`, a summed score makes the duplicated span appear far newer than its real end timestamp and biases eviction away from legitimately-old spans, breaking the stated 'evict oldest end timestamps' contract. Use ZUNIONSTORE ... AGGREGATE MIN (or MAX) so a duplicate keeps a single end timestamp score rather than doubling it.

ZUNIONSTORE uses its default SUM aggregation, so replayed payloads present in both the temporary parent_key and the resolved set_key receive the sum of their end timestamps. Replaying a child whose parent already redirects to an ancestor therefore makes that old span score roughly twice its actual timestamp, protecting it from eviction over genuinely newer spans. Use AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN for identical timestamp scores) on both union operations to preserve timestamp scores when members overlap.

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM, so a payload present in both the destination and source has its timestamp doubled rather than preserved. This can happen when a previously merged span is replayed into its original subtree key. The duplicated span then sorts after genuinely newer spans and survives ZPOPMIN eviction incorrectly. Specify AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN, since identical payloads should have identical timestamps) on both union calls so merging remains idempotent and scores remain end timestamps.

issues.descricao: Segment keys change from Redis sets to sorted sets under the same key names, so keys left by the previous release make ZADD, ZCARD and ZSCAN fail with WRONGTYPE during rollout, crashing span processing and flushing.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Changed SET ops (scard/sunionstore) to ZSET ops (zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin) with no migration breaks in-flight segments. WHY: Old keys of type SET still live up to TTL; ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN/ZADD on the opposite type raises WRONGTYPE and fails inserts/flushes during rollout.

The segment keys were migrated from Redis SETs to SORTED SETs (ZADD/ZSCAN/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN), but nothing handles the keys written by the currently deployed release. During a rolling deploy, an existing `span-buf:s:{...}:{id}` key is still a SET, so this `p.zadd(...)` (and the flusher's `p.zscan(...)`, and the Lua `zcard`/`zunionstore`) raises WRONGTYPE 'Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value'. That exception is unhandled: it aborts the whole pipeline/Lua invocation and crashes the consumer batch. Add a key-schema version to the key name (or a migration/fallback) so old SET-typed keys cannot be touched as sorted sets.

The new ZADD writes sorted sets into the same span-buf:s namespace previously populated by SADD, without migrating existing set keys. During deployment, inserting into an existing buffered segment fails with WRONGTYPE, and the new ZSCAN reader likewise fails on pending old-format segments instead of flushing them. Introduce a coordinated migration/drain or a versioned namespace with compatible handling of pending old-format buffers.

issues.descricao: Claims zpopmin eviction can drop the root span while the has-root flag stays set, flushing a segment without its root.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: zpopmin eviction by lowest end_timestamp has no protection for the segment/root span. WHY: Root with smallest or tied timestamp (tests use identical timestamps, ties break lexicographically) is evicted while hrs flag stays 1, flushing a root-marked segment missing its root.

issues.descricao: max_segment_spans is still a constructor parameter but is no longer enforced; the segment cap is now hardcoded to 1000 in the Lua script, so the configured value is ignored.

comentarios.texto: This hunk removes the only load-time span-count cap (`self.max_segment_spans`): previously a segment exceeding 1001 spans was logged, deleted from `payloads`/`cursors`, and skipped, but now every scanned span is unconditionally appended via `payloads[key].extend(...)`. The new bound relies entirely on insert-time eviction in the Lua script; if that eviction fails to bound a key (e.g. duplicated/scored members or the concurrent-writer case the code itself warns about at lines 457-461), this method will now materialize an unbounded number of spans into memory and emit them, whereas before it was safely skipped. Re-introduce a span-count guard (or verify the invite-time eviction strictly caps cardinality) to keep memory bounded.

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because the test patches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so nothing waits for the flusher threads before `step.join()` and the `messages` assertion. issues.descricao: The restart path only kills a hung flusher if it is a multiprocessing.Process, but spawn-context workers are SpawnProcess, so hung processes are never killed and a duplicate flusher is started for the same shards.
issues.textoGolden: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

comentarios.texto: The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard does not match the SpawnProcess instances created by self.mp_context.Process. When a worker hangs, the guard skips kill() and the replacement starts while the original worker remains alive, allowing overlapping flushing of the same shards if the original resumes and leaking hung workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or self.mp_context.Process, and kill and join the old worker before replacing it.

The workers are created with get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances; these are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class). Consequently this guard skips kill() for actual production workers. When a worker hangs, the replacement starts while the original remains alive and can resume flushing the same shards. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or the spawn-context Process class for the check, and fix the identical check in join() so shutdown also terminates surviving workers.

Workers created by multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process are SpawnProcess instances, not instances of the separate multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently this guard skips kill() for production workers. When a live worker exceeds max-unhealthy-seconds, the code starts a replacement and overwrites its handle while the original is still running. If the original resumes, both workers flush the same shards, and repeated hangs can exceed the configured process limit. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or explicitly distinguish threads) and stop the old worker before replacing it.

issues.descricao: join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping termination of the remaining flusher processes and leaving them running after shutdown.
issues.textoGolden: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

comentarios.texto: join() breaks out of the worker loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping cleanup for every remaining worker. If next_step.join consumes the timeout or an earlier worker exhausts it, remaining flushers can continue running after shutdown or partition reassignment. Use the deadline only to limit waiting and still terminate and reap every remaining process.

Do not break out of worker cleanup when the join deadline expires. If the first worker consumes the timeout, the next iteration breaks before terminating that worker or any subsequent workers. They may still be blocked in Redis or producer calls despite the shared stopped flag, leaving old workers running after strategy shutdown/reassignment. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of remaining time (using a type check that recognizes spawn-context workers).
join() waits for processes sequentially against a single shared deadline and breaks without terminating remaining processes once it expires, leaking them.

issues.descricao: The SpanFlusher docstring says it creates one process per shard, but shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

comentarios.texto: The docstring says the flusher "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the code at lines 60-66 shares shards across a capped number of processes (num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)); each shard assigned via i % self.num_processes). With the new --flusher-processes default of 1, a single process handles every shard, so the documented contract is the opposite of the behaviour this PR introduces (confirmed by test_flusher_processes_limit, which asserts 4 shards served by 2 processes). Update the docstring to say shards are distributed across up to max_processes flusher processes.

The new docstring says this creates one process per shard, but workers are capped by max_processes and shards are distributed among them. In particular, the CLI default of 1 means all assigned shards share one process. Describe capped workers with potentially multiple shards per worker so callers do not rely on per-shard process isolation.

The docstring says the flusher 'Creates one process per shard', but the number of processes is capped by max_processes (--flusher-processes), and shards are shared across processes via i % num_processes. Reword it to say that shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

issues.descricao: max_processes uses a truthiness fallback, so --flusher-processes 0 silently becomes one process per shard instead of being rejected.

comentarios.texto: `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a falsy value as 'not provided'. The new `--flusher-processes` click option is `type=int`, so a user can pass `0`; that legitimate-but-falsy value is discarded and the flusher silently spawns one process per shard instead of honoring the requested limit. Use an explicit None check, e.g. `self.max_processes = max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and validate/reject 0 upstream).

An explicit max_processes=0 is treated as an omitted limit by `or`, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` starts one process per assigned shard instead of respecting or rejecting the supplied zero limit. The CLI accepts zero as an integer and the factory forwards it unchanged. Default only when max_processes is None, and explicitly validate that supplied process limits are positive so zero cannot silently enable potentially many workers.

`max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses a truthiness test, so an explicit 0 is treated as 'unset' and silently expands to one process per shard. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and reject values below 1.

issues.descricao: A negative --flusher-processes value is not validated and makes SpanFlusher construction fail with KeyError.

comentarios.texto: `flusher_processes` is not validated to be >= 1. `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` lets a negative value through (it is truthy), so `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` becomes negative and `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, leaving `process_to_shards_map` as `{}`. The following loop computes `process_index = i % self.num_processes`, which for any negative divisor is 0, so `self.process_to_shards_map[0].append(shard)` raises KeyError and the consumer fails to construct. Since `flusher_processes` is exposed as an int CLI option (`--flusher-processes`), a negative value is reachable from configuration. Guard with `max(1, self.num_processes)` / validate the input.
negative max_processes flows through `or` guard into min() -> empty map -> KeyError on i % num_processes; empty assigned_shards yields zero processes.

issues.descricao: submit() queries cluster-wide Redis memory once per flusher buffer, repeating identical INFO calls per process on every submit.

comentarios.texto: The new loop calls get_memory_info() once per flusher buffer even though SpansBuffer.get_memory_info delegates to iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client), which fetches INFO for the entire Redis cluster regardless of assigned_shards. With P flusher processes and memory backpressure enabled, each submitted batch now performs P identical cluster-wide memory queries on the consumer thread instead of one, increasing Redis traffic and blocking ingestion. Fetch cluster memory information once from a single buffer.
submit() loop calls buffer.get_memory_info() per flusher but each call is cluster-wide from same client, repeating identical INFO N× per submit.

issues.descricao: _create_process_for_shard is added but never called.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is newly added but has no caller anywhere (grep for `_create_process_for_shard(` finds only its definition); the restart path actually used is `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. WHY: This is dead code that indicates the intended per-shard restart wiring was left incomplete — any future caller relying on restarting only the process owning a given shard will silently do nothing, and it is confusing which restart path is authoritative. HOW: Remove `_create_process_for_shard`, or wire it into `_ensure_processes_alive` if per-shard restart was intended.

issues.descricao: test_flusher_processes_limit counts assigned shards instead of checking that each shard is assigned exactly once.

comentarios.texto: The assertion counts shard entries rather than verifying shard assignment. A broken distribution such as {0: [0, 1], 1: [0, 1]} still passes all assertions in this test while shards 2 and 3 are never flushed. Assert that the flattened mapping contains exactly the expected assigned shards, with no duplicates (and verify each worker's shard buffer uses that mapping), rather than only asserting a total of four.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: Narrowing the cache lock to only `b.cache[key] = idx` makes cache entries observable in the middle of a build, so two concurrent builds for the same `NamespacedResource` can run simultaneously and the later one overwrites the first. WHY: A reader that already fetched the first index keeps using it after `b.cache[key]` is reassigned, so subsequent writes/deletes handled by the second index are silently ignored by that reader (and both builders create/overwrite the same on-disk directory under `b.opts.Root`). HOW: Before building, re-check `b.cache[key]` under `b.cacheMu` and return the existing index, or keep a per-key in-flight lock (e.g. keyed singleflight) so only one build per key is in flight while still allowing builds for different keys to proceed in parallel.

issues.descricao: BuildIndex now locks only the final cache assignment, so concurrent callers for the same uncached key all build the same expensive index in parallel and the last one overwrites the others.
issues.textoGolden: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Removing the function-wide `b.cacheMu.Lock()/defer Unlock()` and keeping only the lock around `b.cache[key]=idx` removes the only thing that serialized GetIndex against an in-flight build. WHY: getOrCreateIndex (resource/search.go:287-307) does GetIndex -> if nil -> build; previously BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole body so a concurrent caller's GetIndex (RLock) blocked until the first build cached the index and then saw it (no second build). Now GetIndex can return nil while a build for the same key is still running, so two requests/watch events build the SAME key concurrently — producing two distinct index instances where the caller holding the non-cached one never observes later writes (stale search results), and, for file-backed indices (size > FileThreshold), two concurrent `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` opening the same on-disk directory. HOW: guard the build per key (e.g. re-check the cache under the write lock after acquiring it, or use a per-key single-flight/lock so only one build runs per NamespacedResource), rather than relying on a global write lock held for the entire body.

The cache mutex was moved to cover only the cache assignment, removing the serialization that previously surrounded the whole BuildIndex. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can now both construct an index (including `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same on-disk path) and both write `b.cache[key]`; the second overwrites the first, so callers get distinct index instances for one key and writes made through the losing instance are invisible to readers of the cached one (and the file-backed build may collide on the same directory). Keep the build for a given key serialized (e.g. restore the lock around the build, or take a per-key lock) instead of locking only the map write.

Locking only cache publication allows concurrent requests for the same uncached key to build separate indexes and overwrite each other's cache entries. Search and handleEvent both call getOrCreateIndex, whose GetIndex previously blocked behind the build-wide lock; now an event can update one newly built index before another build replaces it, losing that update from subsequent search results and leaving the discarded index open. Serialize builds per NamespacedResource and recheck the cache after acquiring that per-key guard.

issues.descricao: The new startup log calls TotalDocs, which iterates the index cache without a lock, after the event goroutine that can add indexes has started, so a concurrent map read and write can crash the process.
issues.textoGolden: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

comentarios.texto: The newly added `s.search.TotalDocs()` call is unsafe: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:144-150) iterates `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`, while the bleve.go hunk in this same PR keeps `cacheMu` for the `b.cache[key] = idx` write only. Because search.go:207-213 already started the watch-event goroutine that can call `build` → `BuildIndex` → cache write, line 216 can iterate the map concurrently with that write, causing a `concurrent map iteration and map write` panic or data race. Either guard the `TotalDocs` read with `cacheMu`, or move this call to a point where no build can run concurrently.

The new startup log calls TotalDocs after launching the write-event listener, but bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu.RLock. A write event for an unindexed resource can concurrently publish an index through BuildIndex, causing a map iteration/write race and potentially a fatal runtime error during initialization. Protect TotalDocs cache iteration with the same read lock used by GetIndex.

BuildIndex now writes b.cache under Lock while TotalDocs (called from search.init after the watch goroutine starts) ranges over b.cache without any lock. This can cause a concurrent map read/write fatal error. Fix by taking cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

issues.descricao: NewResourceServer returns an error when Init fails without cancelling the server context created earlier.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and, on error, returns `nil, err` without invoking the `cancel` func created at line 229 and without running any lifecycle cleanup. WHY: Init may have already started long-lived goroutines — searchSupport.init's event-consumption loop uses context.Background() (resource/search.go:202) and initWatcher starts a watcher bound to s.ctx (server.go:752-770) — so if search.init succeeds and initWatcher (or a later step) fails, the constructor discards the server while those goroutines keep running with no way to stop them, leaking the internal context and watcher goroutines. HOW: on the error path call `cancel()` (and any needed lifecycle.Stop) before returning, or defer the cancel until success.

WHAT: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously but returns nil,err without calling the cancel created for s.ctx. WHY: Failed startup leaks the server context (and any lifecycle/watch resources partially started by Init), leaving goroutines/channel watches alive. HOW: On Init error call s.cancel() (and lifecycle Stop cleanup) before returning.
